item.title: Steering electrons with extreme ultraviolet light—team achieves quantum coherent control
item.description: Light is one of the most powerful tools scientists have for probing matter. By interacting with electrons, light reveals how atoms, molecules and materials are structured and how they evolve in time. Highly energetic ultraviolet and X-ray photons are particularly attractive because they can access electrons located close to atomic nuclei, where each chemical element carries its own distinctive electronic fingerprint.

item.title: Quantum probability can't be derived without assuming it first
item.description: For nearly a century, physicists have relied on the Born rule to calculate the chances of different outcomes when they measure a quantum system. Yet despite decades of effort, nobody has managed to derive the rule from more basic mathematical principles without making assumptions about probability along the way.

item.title: A new way to detect stabilizing properties of optical devices
item.description: In optical fibers, chips and other light-guiding devices, minor defects can scatter photons and disrupt their path. A new study demonstrates a way to reveal properties which, in certain systems, help light wave behavior withstand such flaws. The method could help speed up the search for new kinds of electronics and optical technologies, and contribute to more reliable quantum devices.

item.title: Physicists prove a long-suspected quantum speed limit for thermalization
item.description: Whether we are waiting for a car windshield to defrost in winter or a warm drink to cool down, how long it takes for an object to settle into a stable, even temperature within its environment (thermal equilibrium) depends on numerous factors. These can include surface area, the material properties of an object and airflow.

item.title: Perovskite laser maintains stable performance over 400 million pulses
item.description: In a study published in Advanced Optical Materials, researchers at Vilnius University (VU) demonstrated perovskite-based laser structures that maintained stable performance over more than 400 million pulses. Their findings address one of the major challenges limiting the practical use of perovskites: their instability. These semiconductor materials could play an important role in next-generation optical technologies, but their tendency to degrade has long posed a challenge for researchers worldw

item.title: X-ray free-electron laser sets new record for shortest high-energy pulses
item.description: Researchers at the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS) at the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have measured the shortest high-energy X-ray pulses ever recorded at an X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL). The pulses had photon energies of about 9 kiloelectronvolts (keV) and clocked in at durations of 100 to 400 attoseconds—mere billionths of a billionth of a second. The results are published in Nature Photonics.

item.title: 诺奖颁给冰立方：“天马行空的想法，值得被支持几十年”
item.description: 2026年10月6日，冰立方中微子天文台（IceCube）项目发起人弗朗西斯·哈尔岑（Francis Halzen）获得诺贝尔物理学奖。

item.title: “冰立方”为何获得2026诺贝尔物理奖？现场对话诺奖评委
item.description: 1988年，弗朗西斯·哈尔岑（Francis Halzen）提出一个构想，利用南极深处的冰层探测来自宇宙的中微子。二十多年后，这一构想成为覆盖一立方公里冰层的冰立方（IceCube）中微子天文台。借助埋在冰中的光传感器，研究人员捕捉到了具有天体物理起源的高能中微子，为研究遥远宇宙中的高能过程提供了新的观测途径。

item.title: Lost Schrödinger manuscript reveals his true view of quantum randomness
item.description: Unlike classical physics, quantum mechanics generally cannot tell us exactly what will happen in an individual event. Instead, it predicts the probabilities of different outcomes. As one of the theory's early pioneers, Erwin Schrödinger played a key role in debates about what this randomness really means. However, part of his contribution has stayed hidden for more than 80 years.

item.title: Sapphire-grown semiconductor film sets bandgap record
item.description: Semiconductors with wider bandgaps could pave the way for smaller, more efficient electronics that can handle far higher voltages, but the wider this gap becomes, the harder it is to control how well a material conducts electricity. Now, a team led by Darrell Schlom at Cornell University has shown that adding silicon to thin films of aluminum gallium oxide can keep this control intact at bandgaps wider than any semiconductor before it. Their research has been published in Nature.

item.title: Could consciousness be quantum?
item.description: A controversial idea linking quantum physics and consciousness is moving from speculation towards experiments that could finally put it to the test

item.title: Laser-made lattice reveals discrete light solitons in tunable atomic vapor
item.description: Scientists from the Quantum Technologies Group at the Institute of Physics Zagreb, in collaboration with a colleague from the Physics Department at the Faculty of Science (PMF), have experimentally demonstrated for the first time the existence of discrete one-dimensional (1D) solitons in an optically induced photonic lattice in warm rubidium vapor.

item.title: Ultrafast light can control ferromagnetism without relying on heating
item.description: Despite being known for more mundane uses such as sticking notes to refrigerators or keeping bags shut, magnetization is one of the most fundamental and useful properties of a material. Indeed, it forms the physical basis for storing most of our digital information, encoding the bits used in hard drives, computer memories and credit cards.

item.title: 'Invisible' tweak could help make protein shakes less clumpy
item.description: Scientists from RMIT University and Riga Technical University in Latvia have shown that static charge left on surfaces can be controlled, which may have big benefits for companies needing to avoid the little zap in production of common household goods. The discovery could even one day help stop powders such as protein, chocolate malt powders and coffee from clumping.

item.title: See Inside Cells Like Never Before in These Vivid Microscopic Images
item.description: Winning entries in the 2026 Nikon Small World competitions reveal the hidden interactions that govern everyday life. The post See Inside Cells Like Never Before in These Vivid Microscopic Images first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Atomic memory keeps distant ions entangled for about 10 seconds
item.description: Quantum networks, systems that connect devices and allow them to exchange information encoded in the quantum states of particles, could enable more secure communications. To build these networks, physicists need to devise strategies that allow distant particles to share quantum states, preserving them long enough to perform calculations or enable communication between devices.

item.title: A hidden rivalry between two quantum states at the heart of superconductors
item.description: Transmitting electricity without losing any energy may sound impossible, yet this is precisely the promise of superconductivity. For nearly 40 years, scientists have been working to understand materials that exhibit this remarkable property at relatively high temperatures. Unlocking their secrets could one day help make power grids more efficient, enhance medical technologies and support the development of quantum computing.

item.title: Oxygen collisions show evidence of jet quenching, a signature of early-universe matter
item.description: New results from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) provide strong evidence that smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light generates a quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a type of matter that existed just after the birth of the universe. The data, just published in Physical Review Letters, show that energetic jets of particles lose energy as they traverse the hot, dense matter left in the collision's wake.

item.title: Custom frame timing captures ultrafast events across five orders of magnitude in time
item.description: Most conventional methods of ultrafast photography use evenly spaced intervals in which images are taken, but new developments have shown how much can be left out of the story, especially when multiple timescales are involved.

item.title: 2026诺贝尔化学奖给了法国95岁学者和日本75岁学者，日本科学诺奖得主已有28位
item.description: 10月7日，2026年诺贝尔化学奖授予亨利·卡根（Henri B. Kagan）和硤合宪三（Kenso Soai），以表彰他们“发现不对称有机合成中的非线性效应与自催化现象”。2001年，诺贝尔化学奖表彰不对称催化研究，获奖者为威廉·诺尔斯、野依良治和巴里·夏普莱斯。卡根未获奖，引发法国学界不满，时任法国科研部长致信诺贝尔基金会。《自然》当年报道了这场争议。25年后，95岁的卡根因不对称合成中另一项贡献终获诺奖。

item.title: Individual atomic collisions can now be detected in the lab, potentially opening up pathways to new physics
item.description: Tiny atoms and molecules are constantly bombarding each other all around us. While we regularly measure the large-scale effects of these interactions, measuring the effect of each individual collision is far more difficult. But now, researchers have managed to measure how tiny gas particles affect a single silica particle in the lab. In their new study, published in Physical Review Letters, the team describes how they detected the momentum transfers of individual collisions of gas particles with

item.title: A quantum pathway to entropy-free energy transfer
item.description: For scientists, breakthroughs often stem from unexpected turns. A research team led by Oscar Dahlsten, an associate professor in the Department of Physics at City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK), set out to prove a theoretical limitation, only to discover a quantum solution. The finding breaks traditional physical constraints and introduces a strategy for harvesting energy from fluctuating sources.

item.title: Forgotten particle could answer mystery of why we exist, say physicists
item.description: Scientists have unveiled a new theory on the birth of the cosmos, suggesting the early universe was shaped by an ancient particle that has been overlooked for decades.

item.title: Scientists redetermine a key strontium frequency with 50 times better precision for quantum technologies
item.description: The Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS) has remeasured a key transition frequency of the strontium (Sr) atom for the first time in 88 years, since 1938, using a photonic grating chip. It has established a new absolute frequency value with a measurement uncertainty reduced by more than 50 times. By providing an accurate reference value for next-generation quantum technologies, this achievement is expected to contribute to the precise control and miniaturization of quantum de

item.title: X-rays reveal surprisingly long-lived spin waves in copper oxide
item.description: Today's computer technology, based on silicon chips, is slowly reaching its physical limits. Components cannot be miniaturized indefinitely, and clock speeds cannot be increased indefinitely. At the same time, huge AI data centers are being built in many places, and these consume an immense amount of electricity. This is why scientists around the world are searching for novel materials that can replace or complement silicon technology and consume significantly less electricity.

item.title: AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now?
item.description: Unlike other recent AI proofs, this one has been unpacked by human experts. The implications, one mathematician said, are “staggering.” The post AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Hybrid diamond chip strengthens interactions between light and quantum bits
item.description: Researchers have developed and demonstrated a new hybrid photonic platform that integrates quantum emitters with photonic devices, providing a way to reliably control the interaction between photons and quantum information carriers. The chip-based platform, which combines gallium phosphide (GaP) with a diamond substrate, could help make quantum networks more practical by providing a way to connect quantum devices over long distances.

item.title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
item.description: Moritz Hardt, author of a new book on benchmarks, believes these “standardized tests” for artificial intelligence are fundamentally broken — but not unfixable. The post He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Scientists have just voted to abolish leap seconds
item.description: Since 1972, officials have added 27 leap seconds to the universal clock, but in a meeting this week in France they have decided to abandon the practice

item.title: Will physics be the next field to be turned upside down by AI?
item.description: AI has taken huge strides in computer programming and mathematics – physics could be next
